title: Bonded Titles for Mobile and Manufactured Homes
excerpt: A manufactured home is titled like a vehicle in most states, which means a missing title can be replaced with a surety bond the same way a car's can.
metaDescription: How a bonded title works for a mobile or manufactured home: when it applies, how the bond amount is set, and what changes once the home is affixed to land.

body.text: In most states a manufactured home is titled the same way a vehicle is, through the motor vehicle agency rather than the land records office. That means a missing or defective title can be replaced with a certificate of title bond exactly as a car's can, and the process is close to identical.

items: A home bought from a private seller who never handed over the title.
A home inherited, where the title cannot be found among the paperwork.

A title lost during a move between parks or across state lines, which is one of the cases in [what to do if you have lost the title](/what-to-do-if-youve-lost-the-title-to-your-car-boat-or-rv-understanding-title-bonds).
A home acquired through a park's abandonment process.
An older home that was titled decades ago and whose record has gone missing.

body.text: How the bond amount is set

As with a vehicle, the bond is a multiple of the home's value, and the state decides both the multiplier and how the value is established. Valuing a manufactured home is less standardised than valuing a car: a national price guide may exist for the make and model year, but appraisals are more commonly required, particularly for older homes.
Premiums follow the same structure as any title bond, typically 1.5% of the bond amount with a $100 minimum, and [no credit check under $30,000](/can-you-get-a-bonded-title-with-bad-credit).
The one thing that changes everything

If the home has been permanently affixed to land and the title has been surrendered or retired, it is no longer titled property. At that point it is part of the real estate, and a missing document is a real property matter rather than a title bond one. The remedy there is a title company and possibly a quiet title action, not a surety bond.

So the first question is always whether the home is still titled. If the state's motor vehicle agency still holds a record for it, a bonded title is the route. If the title was retired when the home was set on a foundation, it is not.

Have the home's year, make, model and serial or VIN number ready, along with whatever evidence of ownership you hold, such as a bill of sale or park records. Requirements differ by state, so check your state's page for the multiplier, the accepted valuation method and the bond term, and see [how to get a bonded title](/how-to-get-a-bonded-title) for the process itself.
